  <title>Remarks at Frontier Forum on Super Intelligence</title>
  <link>https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/SpeechesTestimony/opaselig14</link>
  <description>
<span>Remarks at Frontier Forum on Super Intelligence</span>

            <div class="field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field--item"><div><p>Thank you, Michael.</p><p>Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to our inaugural Frontier Forum.</p><p>I want to thank our distinguished panelists and moderators for joining us today, as well as the Innovation Task Force for organizing this forum. Before I provide my opening remarks, I must note that the views I share today are my own as Chairman and don’t necessarily reflect those of the Commission.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Intelligent Regulation</strong></p><p>We’re gathered here today to discuss a technology that’s rapidly transforming the financial markets. President Trump calls it “super intelligence,” or SI, – because “it’s not artificial.”<a href="#_ftn1" name="_ftnref1" title>[1]</a> It’s as real as the printing press, the steam engine, and the internet.</p><p>Like the generational technologies that preceded it, super intelligence promises to reshape our financial markets by continuing a decades-long evolution toward increasingly autonomous trading systems. Fortunately, automated trading is nothing new to the Commission. Some of the earliest algorithmic strategies deployed in our derivatives markets date back to the launch of S&amp;P 500 index futures on designated contract markets in the eighties. Of course, the rise of automated trading was not without controversy. About a decade ago, following the May 2010 Flash Crash, Knight Capital’s runaway algorithm in August 2012, and a sharp disruption in Treasury futures in October 2014, the Commission considered special risk control rules for algorithmic trading firms in a proposal known as Regulation Automated Trading.<a href="#_ftn2" name="_ftnref2" title>[2]</a> The Commission expressed concern that “[m]alfunctioning or incorrectly deployed algorithms deploying erroneous messages to trading venues can significantly impact markets and market participants.”<a href="#_ftn3" name="_ftnref3" title>[3]</a> We hear many of these same concerns today.</p><p>Yet a lot has changed since the Commission proposed the rule, which it never finalized and would be ill-suited for today’s landscape. SI is no longer a tool available only to sophisticated firms and individuals. It’s become nearly as commonplace on our computers and personal devices as a web browser or word processor.</p><p>Many of the most popular SI applications, such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, can interoperate with third-party applications to analyze market data, identify trends, and help users become more informed. Brokerages are also beginning to incorporate SI tools into their customer offerings, putting capabilities once reserved for Wall Street’s largest institutions into the hands of everyday Americans. Meanwhile, individuals are increasingly giving the credentials to their brokerage and bank accounts to their SI agent and trusting the agent to manage their finances. And blockchains are providing rails for autonomous agents to custody and trade crypto assets without relying on banks, brokerages, or other traditional intermediaries.</p><p>It’s no longer science fiction to imagine your refrigerator autonomously purchasing your groceries with funds that it earned from staking ether or launching a meme coin.</p><p>We have to think long and hard about how to regulate intelligently in this age of super intelligence. Like the printing press, the steam engine, and the internet before it, SI will transform the global economy. But America cannot afford to sit idly by as this transformation takes place all around us. It must lead with rational rules that promote technological innovation while also ensuring that our markets remain the deepest and most liquid in the world. We cannot accept the false choice of winning the SI race <em>or</em> maintaining global financial market supremacy. We must do both. And under President Trump’s leadership, we’re doing exactly that.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>SI and the Future of Derivatives Markets</strong></p><p>At their core, derivatives markets serve an essential economic purpose. They help businesses manage risk, discover prices, and make investment decisions with greater confidence. A farmer can hedge the future price of a crop before harvest. An airline can manage its exposure to variable fuel expenses. A manufacturer can protect itself against fluctuations in the cost of raw materials.</p><p>SI has the potential to make risk management more efficient. Consider what it takes to assess risk in modern financial markets. A market participant may need to evaluate thousands of instruments, monitor changing market conditions, and understand how a shock in one market could affect positions across several others.</p><p>That is an enormous amount of information to process, and the consequences of missing something could be detrimental. SI can help process the vast amount of information significantly faster than human brain power and with greater accuracy. For large, institutional firms, that could mean better-informed decisions and more effective risk management. For smaller market participants, it could mean access to capabilities that previously required the resources of a much larger institution.</p><p>That last point is particularly important. Innovation should create opportunities for more Americans and American businesses to participate in our markets.</p><p>By lowering the cost of sophisticated analysis and making powerful tools more widely available, SI could help level the playing field and expand access to risk-management capabilities. It could also improve price discovery by helping market participants better understand the information driving prices and the relationships between different markets.</p><p>These are meaningful opportunities. More effective risk management, better information, and broader access to financial tools will help our derivatives markets serve businesses across the economy even more effectively.</p><p>And as these technologies advance, we should be thinking not just about how SI can improve the markets we have today, but also about the new financial activity it could create.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Agentic Finance</strong></p><p>The CFTC’s regulatory framework was developed around identifiable market participants, intermediaries, and institutions performing specific financial functions.</p><p>But what happens when those functions are increasingly performed or facilitated by autonomous software? Consider an SI agent that identifies trading opportunities and executes transactions on behalf of a user. Does the developer of that agent become subject to registration? Who is liable if the agent goes rogue? How can regulators know who the agent, or suite of agents, is trading on behalf of? Do we need a new flavor of know-your-customer, maybe KYA or know-your-agent?</p><p>These are precisely the types of questions that we face as agentic finance continues to develop in our markets.</p><p>While they are challenging, the CFTC benefits from already having confronted similar issues in crypto asset markets. For years, software developers and entrepreneurs faced uncertainty about whether publishing code or developing user interfaces could trigger regulatory requirements designed for traditional financial intermediaries. Under my leadership, we have strived to provide greater clarity around these questions.</p><p>But as agents become more capable, these distinctions will become increasingly important. Our approach must remain grounded in the functions performed, the control exercised, and the economic realities of the transaction.</p><p>We must also understand the risks that increasingly autonomous systems may introduce. SI agents may respond to market conditions in unexpected ways. Systems relying on similar models may generate correlated trading behavior. And the speed of autonomous transactions may create new challenges for market surveillance and risk management.</p><p>But these technologies also offer opportunities to strengthen market integrity.</p><p>SI systems can help exchanges identify suspicious activity, enable clearinghouses to monitor exposures more effectively, and improve regulators’ ability to detect misconduct. The CFTC is leaning in. Our staff here at the Commission are already using SI to police the markets more effectively than ever before.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Compute Will Power the SI Revolution</strong></p><p>There is another dimension of this transformation that falls squarely within the CFTC’s expertise. Every technological revolution depends on the resources necessary to power it.</p><p>The industrial revolution depended on coal, iron, and steam power. The twentieth century saw the rise of oil, electricity, and modern industrial infrastructure. The SI revolution depends on computational power, or “compute.” Advanced SI systems require enormous amounts of compute, specialized processors, electricity, and data center infrastructure. As demand for these resources grows, businesses will increasingly need tools to manage exposure to changing prices and availability.</p><p>This is the role America’s derivatives markets have played for generations. Farmers hedge agricultural production. Airlines hedge fuel costs. Manufacturers manage exposure to industrial commodities. In the SI economy, developers, infrastructure providers, cyber security firms, and frontier investors may need similar tools to manage SI-related risks.</p><p>Earlier this year, the CFTC sought public comment on the development of compute derivatives markets. We want to understand how these markets are evolving and how our regulatory framework can support their responsible development. The response has been substantial, with more than 100 commenters weighing in on the risks and opportunities these markets present. The CFTC has an opportunity to help establish the financial infrastructure of the SI economy, and we intend to take that opportunity seriously.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>*&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *</strong></p><p>Nearly seventy years ago, an IBM computer scientist named Arthur L. Samuel taught a computer to play checkers, helping establish the principle that machines could do more than just follow instructions.<a href="#_ftn4" name="_ftnref4" title>[4]</a> I suspect he could have scarcely imagined a world in which intelligent systems might one day manage financial portfolios, hedge commodity exposures, and transact directly with one another.</p><p>But that’s the Rubicon we've crossed. And it’s why conversations like today’s are so important. The convergence of super intelligence, crypto, and modern financial infrastructure could transform how our markets have long operated.</p><p>It could expand access to sophisticated financial tools, enable businesses to manage risk with greater precision, and create entirely new forms of economic activity. But realizing that potential will require thoughtful engagement between the innovators building these technologies and the policymakers responsible for overseeing our markets.</p><p>And that is precisely what we hope to accomplish today. Our first panel will explore the implications of SI in the derivatives markets, including how increasingly capable systems may transform trading, price discovery, and risk management. Our second panel will examine the emergence of agentic trading and the questions raised by autonomous systems capable of conducting financial transactions.</p><p>As many of you have already done, I encourage our panelists to challenge conventional thinking, engage candidly about the opportunities and risks, and help us better understand what the next generation of markets may look like.</p><p>At the CFTC, we are committed to ensuring that America’s derivatives markets remain the most innovative, competitive, and resilient in the world.</p><p>We will not sacrifice our global competitive edge in financial markets for the sake of technological supremacy. We will remain the financial capital of the world by embracing this technology and modernizing our approach to regulation for the new frontier of finance.</p><p>Thank you, and I look forward to today’s discussions.</p></div><div><hr align="left" size="1" width="33%"><div id="ftn1"><p><a href="#_ftnref1" name="_ftn1" title><span style="font-size:10pt;">[1]</span></a><span style="font-size:10pt;"> Donald Trump, </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">Transcript: Donald Trump’s Address at ‘Winning the AI Race’ Event</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;">, TechPolicy.Press (July 24, 2025), https://www.techpolicy.press/transcript-donald-trumps-address-at-winning-the-ai-race-event/.</span></p></div><div id="ftn2"><p><a href="#_ftnref2" name="_ftn2" title><span style="font-size:10pt;">[2]</span></a><span style="font-size:10pt;"> Regulation Automated Trading, 80 Fed. Reg. 78824 (proposed Dec. 17, 2015).</span></p></div><div id="ftn3"><p><a href="#_ftnref3" name="_ftn3" title><span style="font-size:10pt;">[3]</span></a><span style="font-size:10pt;"> </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">Id.</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> at 78841.</span></p></div><div id="ftn4"><p><a href="#_ftnref4" name="_ftn4" title><span style="font-size:10pt;">[4]</span></a><span style="font-size:10pt;"> </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">The Games That Helped AI Evolve</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;">, IBM, https://www.ibm.com/history/early-games (last visited Oct. 27, 2026).</span></p></div></div></div>

  <title>Statement on the Commission’s Approval of a Designated Contract Market’s Listing of a Key Performance Indicator Contract</title>
  <link>https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/SpeechesTestimony/seligstatement102226</link>

<span>Statement on the Commission’s Approval of a Designated Contract Market’s Listing of a Key Performance Indicator Contract</span>

            <div class="field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field--item"><p>Today, in response to a request for review and approval under Commission Regulation 40.3, the Commission voted to approve a designated contract market (“DCM”) to list for trading a swap with settlement based on a key performance indicator (the “KPI Contract”).</p><p>As described in the approval order, the KPI Contract is a cash-settled, binary outcome contract structured as a swap under the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”). It is listed and traded on a DCM and cleared through a registered derivatives clearing organization. The KPI Contract—and other similar contracts listed for trading by this and other DCMs— are fully subject to the protections afforded by the CEA and the Commission’s regulations thereunder, including the DCM Core Principles.</p><p>As the order emphasizes, the order speaks solely to the listing and trading of the KPI Contract — and other KPI event contracts discussed in the Submission — structured to trade on a DCM in compliance with the CEA and the Commission’s regulations. The order does not address what may be similar products with the same underlying KPIs structured in different ways. Today’s approval order does not address — and does not foreclose — SEC jurisdiction over KPI contracts based on the same underlying KPIs as those contemplated in the approval order that are structured to fall under the SEC’s jurisdiction. Indeed, our sister agency recognized as much in its own approval order issued earlier this month.</p><p>I join SEC Chairman Atkins in celebrating the end of decades-long jurisdictional “turf wars” between the CFTC and the SEC that have frustrated innovation and left a void of unrealized financial products in their wake. Today’s approval order, along with the SEC’s order, reflects a new spirit of harmonization, innovation, and market participant choice, removing unnecessary obstacles to the lawful introduction of novel financial instruments within our markets.</p><p>I also thank the staff for their hard work and dedication in developing the approval order.</p></div>

  <title>Remarks at Agricultural Commodity Futures Conference</title>
  <link>https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/SpeechesTestimony/opaselig13</link>
  <description>
<span>Remarks at Agricultural Commodity Futures Conference</span>

            <div class="field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field--item"><div><p id="location-date">Good afternoon, everyone. It’s great to be here in Kansas for AgCon. I want to thank Kansas State University President Richard Linton, Director of the K-State Risk Management Center Joe Parcell, and everyone who helped make the return of this great conference a reality. Before I provide my opening remarks, I must note that the views I share today are my own as Chairman and don’t necessarily reflect those of the Commission,</p><p>When we announced that we were bringing AgCon back, we said we wanted this to be a gathering where the CFTC staff could listen and learn about issues facing producers and agribusinesses, activity in the markets, and how to better ensure that end users have the risk management tools they need to hedge their risks. We want this to be a conference that addresses the topics that our agricultural stakeholders actually face – and that’s exactly what we intend to do throughout the course of this conference.</p><p>Some of my predecessors would count a tour of an Impossible Meat processing facility an “ag visit.” My definition’s a bit different: I have instead spent a lot of time this year traveling around the country and talking to farmers and ranchers working hard each day to provide the food, feed, and fiber we depend on throughout our country and the world. I’ve met with farmers, ranchers, agribusinesses, and energy producers in Iowa, Texas, Nebraska, South Carolina, and Florida, and now, I’m with all of you here in Kansas.</p><p>All these meetings have reminded me of one thing: Agriculture is not just another market the CFTC happens to regulate. Agriculture is part of the foundation of why this agency exists in the first place.</p><p>We don’t take the same approach to regulation in agriculture as we do in say crypto or precious metals. The agency understands that livestock production and marketing is different than row crops and specialty crops. Agriculture is regional and affects the Midwest differently than the South or Northeast. We’re working to tailor our regulations to make sure our markets work for everyone.</p><p>To ensure we hear from producers and agribusinesses directly to guide our approach, I reconstituted the CFTC’s Agricultural Advisory Committee, which had been dormant for years. We had our first meeting in July, and it was a big success.</p><p>We discussed numerous topics including Basel III, access to clearing, potential risk management gaps between CFTC and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) product offerings, 24/7 trading, and perpetual futures.&nbsp; I look forward to diving deeper into all these topics throughout AgCon.</p><p>Additionally, I hired the CFTC’s first ever Senior Agriculture Advisor, Emma Johnston. Emma is the fantastic lead staffer on the Ag Advisory Committee and helped plan AgCon. She regularly meets directly with producers and agribusinesses and advises our team and me on developments in the agricultural markets.</p><p>For generations, futures were primarily used in the agricultural industry and traded via the Chicago Board of Trade. But by the early 1920s, concerns over speculative prices, price manipulation, and a postwar collapse in grain prices intensified calls for federal oversight. In 1922, Congress enacted the Grain Futures Act, recognizing that grain futures prices helped determine what farmers received for their crops and what consumers paid for food nationwide. The law established federal oversight of grain futures exchanges within the USDA, laying the foundation for modern commodity regulation. In 1936, Congress expanded the framework through the Commodity Exchange Act, extending federal oversight beyond grain to other agricultural commodities. Then, in 1974, Congress created the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as an independent agency, extending its jurisdiction to a broader universe of statutory commodities – including virtually everything except onions and motion picture box office receipts.</p><p>Fast forward to today: we now oversee a wide range of markets in agricultural, energy, metals, interest rates, and an increasingly innovative range of financial products. But expanding our jurisdiction did not mean abandoning our roots. I believe that if our markets aren’t working for farmers, ranchers, and producers, then they aren’t working at all.</p><p>In fact, Congress created a special category of “agricultural commodities<a style="font-size:10pt;" href="#_ftn1" name="_ftnref1" title>[1]</a>” within our statute for good reason. Because agricultural commodities are different from other types of products and oftentimes demand disparate regulatory treatment.<a style="font-size:10pt;" href="#_ftn2" name="_ftnref2" title>[2]</a></p><p>Under my leadership, the CFTC has spent a lot of time getting back to its roots and focusing on this important class of agricultural commodities that the Commodity Exchange Act’s framers cared so much about. We want innovation, competition, and new ideas. But innovation should expand the risk management toolbox available to producers, not force them to throw away the tools that already work.</p><p>One of the main topics in agriculture we’ve heard throughout this year, whether in D.C. or while traveling across the country, is 24/7 trading. I’ve been very clear about our approach: just because something works in one market does not mean it automatically works in every market. When exchanges sought to introduce 24/7 contracts, we listened to the people who would have actually used those markets, and we stood up for them. We have made clear that markets in agricultural commodities should not be dragged into a 24/7 model simply because the technology exists to make it possible. The Commission will not take a one-size-fits-all approach to 24/7 trading, and I’ve said repeatedly that agricultural commodities may not be appropriate for continuous trading as seen in perpetual contracts.</p><p>We can modernize markets without losing sight of the people those markets were built to serve. That same philosophy extends to data. The Commitment of Traders (COT) report has been an important source of transparency for decades. We heard from the ag community that it can be more useful, so we listened. That’s why we are working internally to publish the COT report twice a week by the end of the year, giving market participants access to more timely information about trading positions and activity in these markets.</p><p>While we take steps to modernize and automate our data for public consumption, we are still abiding by our statutory remit to monitor and surveil the markets for potential manipulation to facilitate sound and efficient markets with fair competition<strong>. </strong>To ensure we have sufficient access to data, we are working closely with the USDA to share information where appropriate, promote transparent markets that enable price discovery, and work with the prudential regulators to streamline capital requirements and foster access to clearing to better serve customers. USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins and her team understand how important well-functioning risk-management markets are to American agriculture. The CFTC and USDA are working toward an updated memorandum of understanding that will strengthen coordination and information sharing between the two agencies and help us better serve farmers, ranchers, and agribusinesses.</p><p>The CFTC is also working with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on issues involving Renewable Identification Numbers, or RINs,&nbsp; carbon credits, and derivatives referencing or economically tied to these products. We are increasing our collaboration with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to ensure we are conducting appropriate oversight of RINs and renewable fuels markets to deter fraud and manipulation, and ensure our markets are safe and competitive for all market participants. The CFTC remains the cop on the beat and seeks to best support our EPA colleagues and the core constituencies of both agencies, the farmer and producer, through fair markets for all market participants. These are exactly the kind of issues that agencies should be talking to one another about rather than operating in silos.</p><p>The same goes for Congress. We have worked with members of both the House and Senate, the White House, and Secretary Rollins to advance policies that address the needs of American farmers, ranchers, and producers. That cooperation is especially important, because the CFTC cannot solve every problem through regulation.</p><p>Under my chairmanship, I’ve made it a priority to refocus the agency on its statutory mission. Gone are the days of using our resources to pursue ESG objectives or climate-policy initiatives that are outside our core responsibilities. Instead, we are focused on market integrity, competition, innovation, and regulating the markets Congress gave us the responsibility to regulate.</p><p>One of those markets is the agricultural commodity futures market. This market is so important that we didn’t just bring CFTC officials here. We brought senior officials from the White House and USDA so they can hear directly from you.</p><p>I look forward to the conversation we will have over the next few days and thank you all for being here today and giving us the opportunity to listen.</p><p>Now, I would like to introduce Dr. Tim Steffensmeier, Assistant Vice President and Director for Engagement and Outreach for Kansas State, to help me open up this conference.</p></div><div><hr align="left" size="1" width="33%"><div id="ftn1"><p><a href="#_ftnref1" name="_ftn1" title><span style="font-size:10pt;">[1]</span></a><span style="font-size:10pt;"> The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, Pub. L. No. 111-203, §§ 721(a)(21), 723(c)(3), 733, 124 Stat. 1376, 1666, 1682, 1712 (2010) (“Dodd-Frank Act”) amended the Commodity Exchange Act to bring agricultural swaps within the statutory definition of a “swap” and to govern transactions in an “agricultural commodity,” as that term is defined by the Commission. In 2011, the Commission finalized the definition of “agricultural commodity” to outline the scope of its subsequent agricultural swaps rulemakings. </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">See</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> Agricultural Commodity Definition, 76 Fed. Reg. 41048 (July 13, 2011) (final rule); Agricultural Commodity Definition, 75 Fed. Reg. 65586 (Oct. 26, 2010) (proposed rule).</span></p></div><div id="ftn2"><p><a href="#_ftnref2" name="_ftn2" title><span style="font-size:10pt;">[2]</span></a><span style="font-size:10pt;"> </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">See, e.g.,</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> Dodd-Frank Act § 723(c)(3), 124 Stat. at 1682 (subjecting agricultural swaps to a unique statutory prohibition not applied to other physical commodities); </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">id.</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> § 737, 124 Stat. at 1722 (establishing a differentiated 270-day timeline for agricultural position limits to accommodate distinct market structures); </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">see also</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> Agricultural Commodity Definition, 76 Fed. Reg. 41048, 41049 (July 13, 2011) (final rule) (reviewing the statutory evolution, including the Dodd-Frank Act’s elimination of prior CEA provisions relating to agricultural commodities and its addition of several new provisions relating to those commodities). </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">Cf.</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> the commercial end-user exception codified in Section 2(h)(7) of the Commodity Exchange Act and implemented in 17 CFR § 50.50, which exempts non-financial entities from mandatory clearing requirements for swaps. Congress designed this carve-out so that commercial market participants (such as farmers) can use over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives to cost-effectively manage business risks without being burdened by central clearing and margin obligations. </span><em><span style="font-size:10pt;">Cf.</span></em><span style="font-size:10pt;"> the commercial end-user exemption from margin requirements on uncleared swaps, codified in Section 4s(e) of the Commodity Exchange Act and implemented by 17 CFR §§ 23.150–23.161, which, working in tandem with the clearing exemption, provides commercial end-users relief from initial and variation margin requirements.</span></p></div></div></div>

  <title>Remarks at the Fordham Law Blockchain Regulatory Symposium</title>
  <link>https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/SpeechesTestimony/opaselig12</link>
  <description>
<span>Remarks at the Fordham Law Blockchain Regulatory Symposium</span>

            <div class="field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field--item"><div><p>Chris, thank you for the kind introduction. It’s great to be back with you in New York City. It feels like just yesterday that we were sitting together talking shop in Willkie’s offices down the street. After having had the opportunity to work with you at the Commission and in private practice, it’s an incredible honor to now follow in your footsteps as Chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). But there will always be only one “CryptoDad.”</p><p>You once said “we owe it to this new generation to respect their enthusiasm about [crypto] with a thoughtful and balanced response, not a dismissive one.”<a href="#_ftn1" name="_ftnref1" title>[1]</a> I hope the regulatory initiatives that I’ll be sharing with you all today demonstrate that the CFTC is committed to doing so.</p><p>But before I begin, I must note that the views I share today are my own as Chairman and don’t necessarily reflect those of the Commission.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Satoshi’s Revolution</strong></p><p>In the wake of the dot-com bubble, Professor Carlota Perez observed in her seminal work <em>Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital</em> that transformational technologies, like the printing press, railroad, and internet, all result in a similar structure of technological revolution. She explained that each revolution begins with the&nbsp;</p><blockquote><p>. . . replacement of one set of technologies by another . . . Investment in the new industries is carried out by new entrepreneurs while the young financial tycoons create a whirlpool that sucks in huge amounts of the world’s wealth to reallocate it in more adventurous or reckless hands . . . Eventually, it has to collapse. But when it does, the changeover has been made. . . . the new way of doing things with new technologies has become ‘common sense.’ . . . Though the debate about the causes and the culprits can go on forever, the more practical task of setting up an adequate regulatory system and a set of effective safeguards is soon undertaken. Thanks to the crash and the recession, there is a newfound readiness to accept such rules on the part of the – until recently arrogant – financial wizards, now sobered up. If, at this turning point, the institutional adjustment is successfully achieved, what follows may be a golden age.<a href="#_ftn2" name="_ftnref2" title>[2]</a></p></blockquote><p>Nearly two decades ago, Satoshi Nakamoto published a white paper called “Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System”<a href="#_ftn3" name="_ftnref3" title>[3]</a> that was the big-bang of a new universe of decentralized networks, applications, and assets. The white paper described a “system based on cryptographic proof instead of trust, allowing any two parties to transact directly with each other without the need for a trusted third party.”<a href="#_ftn4" name="_ftnref4" title>[4]</a> Several months later, Nakamoto released the open-source Bitcoin Core software, creating the very first blockchain network and crypto asset.<a href="#_ftn5" name="_ftnref5" title>[5]</a> Unlike other networks, Bitcoin is decentralized both politically and architecturally – no single person controls it and it has no central point of failure – but it’s logically centralized in that it requires a distributed set of nodes to reach consensus on the system’s state to function as a single virtual computer.<a href="#_ftn6" name="_ftnref6" title>[6]</a></p><p>Bitcoin didn’t immediately catch on.<a href="#_ftn7" name="_ftnref7" title>[7]</a> But soon the software initially adopted solely by “cypherpunks” at the fringes of the technological frontier had inspired a new generation of builders across the world.</p><p>One of those innovators was Vitalik Buterin, who developed his own white paper describing a blockchain network called Ethereum.<a href="#_ftn8" name="_ftnref8" title>[8]</a> Buterin iterated upon Nakamoto’s design for a trust-minimized<a href="#_ftn9" name="_ftnref9" title>[9]</a> virtual computer shared across a network of peers<a href="#_ftn10" name="_ftnref10" title>[10]</a> and created a Turing-complete system that supported programmable smart contracts. Unlike Nakamoto’s bitcoin, Buterin designed Ethereum as a general-purpose protocol that would “allow other decentralized applications to build on top of it.”<a href="#_ftn11" name="_ftnref11" title>[11]</a> The network’s native crypto asset – ether – would serve an essential role as “gas,” required to run transactions on the protocol. Armed with this technology and a new programming language called Solidity, developers across the world set out to create new decentralized applications.</p><p>Blockchain technology “combine[d] the openness of democracy and the Internet with the merit of markets” and made it possible to “port the market model to places where it couldn’t go before.”<a href="#_ftn12" name="_ftnref12" title>[12]</a> A blockchain’s core software, running on each network participant’s hardware, dictates the terms of network consensus and each participant is incentivized to follow these rules, minimizing trust in any individual participant.</p><p>This remedied what Marc Andreessen has referred to as the “original sin” of the internet – its lack of a native property ownership protocol.<a href="#_ftn13" name="_ftnref13" title>[13]</a> As the economist Hernando de Soto has observed, the ability to own property with the assurance that it will not arbitrarily be taken away transforms property into capital and unleashes its potential energy into the broader economy.<a href="#_ftn14" name="_ftnref14" title>[14]</a> In contrast to the offline world, the internet allowed users to read and write, but not to <em>own</em> value without reliance on a trusted party.<a href="#_ftn15" name="_ftnref15" title>[15]</a> Without a native property ownership system, intermediaries stepped in to perform this function and users, startups, and creators were left reliant on centralized platforms that could change the rules on them at any time.<a href="#_ftn16" name="_ftnref16" title>[16]</a> The open and merit-based market model of the blockchain brought permissionless innovation back to the internet, made it possible to own and transfer value without a bank account or subscription service, and turned network users into network stakeholders.<a href="#_ftn17" name="_ftnref17" title>[17]</a></p><p>This new ability to represent virtually anything and everything as a crypto asset on a blockchain led to a “Cambrian explosion”<a href="#_ftn18" name="_ftnref18" title>[18]</a> of crypto assets on general-purpose blockchain networks like Ethereum, Cosmos, and Solana. We saw the invention of entirely new categories of programmable digital objects with varying degrees of external dependencies.<a href="#_ftn19" name="_ftnref19" title>[19]</a> While the very first crypto assets were designed to function as currencies, many that followed were intended to be commodities that performed a specific role in a decentralized network or application and derived their value from network effects. We also saw the “tokenization” of a wide range of real-world assets, such as stocks, dollars, precious metals, and even jpegs.</p><p>Although Nakamoto’s vision was for a virtual economy without trusted intermediaries, centralized crypto asset exchanges and brokerages soon emerged to meet demand for on- and off-ramps to the frontier. Many of the earliest exchanges and brokerages formed offshore before imploding in the wake of devastating cyber-attacks and rampant fraud.<a href="#_ftn20" name="_ftnref20" title>[20]</a> Others chose to attempt to navigate a complex regulatory landscape in the United States.</p><p>After the collapse of a popular offshore exchange, state banking regulators across the country deemed crypto assets to be a form of “money” or “currency” under their respective state money transmission statutes and required exchanges and brokerages to be licensed as money transmitters. State money transmission laws originated in the early 1900s to protect customers of non-bank service providers from fraud and insolvency in connection with remittances and payments.<a href="#_ftn21" name="_ftnref21" title>[21]</a> Exchanges and brokerages soon found themselves licensed in up to fifty states and territories, alongside gift card issuers and check cashers. These state regimes required licensees to perform important functions, such as know-your-customer and anti-money laundering checks, but did not require licensees to institute market-based protections that are typical under federal market regulatory regimes, such as orderly trading requirements, anti-manipulation rules, and mitigation of conflicts of interest. Nor did these regimes contemplate separate licenses and requirements for brokering, dealing, executing, and clearing trades.</p><p>As crypto exploded in popularity, issuers of new crypto assets began to sell their coins directly to the public in what came to be known as “initial coin offerings.”<a href="#_ftn22" name="_ftnref22" title>[22]</a> Without clear rules of the road, consumers had difficulty discerning the legitimate projects from the fraudulent ones, and trouble distinguishing the Pets.com’s from the Amazon’s. Like the dot-com bubble before it, the “ICO” bubble eventually burst, and a “crypto winter” set in. But the builders continued to innovate, designing new network layers, protocols, and products. Winter gave way to “crypto spring” and “defi summer,” and each cycle a new class of builders entered the fray.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>1) What</strong></p><p>When the news broke about FTX, it was a slow drip over hours, days, and weeks. A CoinDesk article questioned the company’s balance sheet.<a href="#_ftn23" name="_ftnref23" title>[23]</a> Another exchange’s chief executive publicly expressed skepticism about the company’s financials. FTX’s founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, followed with the infamous “1) What” tweet.<a href="#_ftn24" name="_ftnref24" title>[24]</a> FTX’s lenders then struggled to figure out what to do with the “FTT” tokens they held as collateral.<a href="#_ftn25" name="_ftnref25" title>[25]</a> Founders and investors frantically called their lawyers and advisors for help. Distressed funds circled the wreckage, picking through FTT and other stranded tokens at collapsed prices as firms raced to salvage whatever value remained. Meanwhile, lawyers and advisors anxiously refreshed their browsers for the latest installment of Matt Levine’s daily coverage of the debacle.<a href="#_ftn26" name="_ftnref26" title>[26]</a></p><p>Eventually it came to light that FTX’s operators stole more than $8 billion in exchange customer assets to engage in their own proprietary investments. Although FTX had a U.S. subsidiary with state money transmitter licenses, its customers’ funds were nowhere to be found. However, the customer property held by FTX’s CFTC-registered subsidiaries remained segregated and secure. A credit to the agency’s robust customer safeguards and market surveillance.</p><p>As Professor Perez observed, eventually the euphoria ends, but when it does “the new way of doing things with new technologies has become ‘common sense.’”<a href="#_ftn27" name="_ftnref27" title>[27]</a> FTX’s implosion reverberated throughout the global crypto markets and ushered in a crypto winter unlike any the industry had seen before, but the technology persevered.</p><p>This is when the American crypto industry learned “[t]he nine most terrifying words in the English language . . . I’m from the Government, and I’m here to help.”<a href="#_ftn28" name="_ftnref28" title>[28]</a></p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Regulation in One Lesson</strong></p><p>Governments across the globe scrambled to respond to FTX’s collapse as crypto asset intermediaries across the world continued to fall. In the ensuing months and years, legislators and regulators convened hearings, roundtables, and studies to support the development of new laws and regulations for crypto markets. Dozens of countries then established comprehensive regulatory regimes. The European Union codified MiCA,<a href="#_ftn29" name="_ftnref29" title>[29]</a> the United Kingdom issued crypto market rules under FSMA,<a href="#_ftn30" name="_ftnref30" title>[30]</a> and Singapore instituted regulations for digital token service providers.<a href="#_ftn31" name="_ftnref31" title>[31]</a></p><p>In the United States, the CFTC and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) took a different approach. The agencies chose to utilize their existing statutory authorities not to write new rules for these markets, but to regulate them by enforcement.</p><p>Before enforcement came to define the federal government’s approach to crypto, both agencies spent half a decade attempting to chart a regulatory path for crypto assets.</p><p>In 2014, former CFTC Chairman Timothy Massad declared bitcoin to be a “commodity” within the Commission’s regulatory scheme.<a href="#_ftn32" name="_ftnref32" title>[32]</a> The CFTC later greenlit the first regulated bitcoin futures contracts under the leadership of former Chairman Chris Giancarlo.<a href="#_ftn33" name="_ftnref33" title>[33]</a> In the years that followed, former Chairman Heath Tarbert set forth his views as Chairman when he deemed ether to be a “commodity” and, under his leadership, the agency finalized interpretive guidance concerning the term “actual delivery” in relation to crypto assets.<a href="#_ftn34" name="_ftnref34" title>[34]</a></p><p>Around this time, the SEC staff followed with a “framework”<a href="#_ftn35" name="_ftnref35" title>[35]</a> on investment contracts involving crypto assets and several no-action letters to crypto asset issuers clarifying that their coin offerings would not be subject to registration with the agency.<a href="#_ftn36" name="_ftnref36" title>[36]</a> With more than 50 subjective factors to navigate, and no further guidance from the SEC, market participants resorted to creating a dedicated “Crypto Rating Council” to score, on a 1-5 scale, the likelihood of a crypto asset being deemed to be a security.<a href="#_ftn37" name="_ftnref37" title>[37]</a> Lawyers started churning out reasoned <em>Howey </em>memos in attempts to untie a Gordian knot of almost a century of case law concerning orange groves, payphones, chinchillas, and condominiums in transactions that bore almost no resemblance to the emergent, decentralized business models that were on the cusp of the new frontier of finance. A boon for lawyers’ billable hours – not so much for American innovators.</p><p>Then, under the Biden administration, the agencies quickly shifted course to regulation by enforcement – a trend that amplified dramatically in the wake of FTX’s downfall. Crypto no-action letters quickly became historical artifacts of a bygone era after regulators closed their doors to productive discussions with market participants.</p><p>The CFTC used its authority over “retail commodity transactions” under section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) to charge several operators of centralized exchanges and developers of decentralized exchange protocols for offering transactions that are required to be executed on a CFTC-registered exchange, known as a designated contract market (or DCM).<a href="#_ftn38" name="_ftnref38" title>[38]</a> The agency proceeded with these investigations and lawsuits despite the lack of clear rules, interpretations, or relief needed to make on-exchange trading of crypto assets possible.</p><p>In one case, the CFTC obtained a default judgment against a decentralized autonomous organization after serving process on the protocol by messaging an online “help chat box” on its website.<a href="#_ftn39" name="_ftnref39" title>[39]</a> In another, the agency fined a software developer for offering a user interface for an automated market maker protocol that enabled users to interact with smart contracts to engage in off-exchange retail commodity transactions.<a href="#_ftn40" name="_ftnref40" title>[40]</a></p><p>The status of a given crypto asset as a “commodity” within the CFTC’s remit could only be determined based upon a review of the non-exhaustive list of assets included in each lawsuit and cross-reference against the copious list of “crypto asset securities” included in the SEC’s lawsuits.<a href="#_ftn41" name="_ftnref41" title>[41]</a> Yet it wasn’t even clear that the heads of the two agencies agreed on which assets were and weren’t securities.</p><p>Under former SEC Chairman Gary Gensler’s leadership, the agency similarly charged operators of centralized exchanges and developers of decentralized protocols with failure to register as broker-dealers and national securities exchanges. He glibly directed new entrants to fill out “a form on our website” to register without making any modifications to the SEC’s rules or regulations to accommodate the technology.<a href="#_ftn42" name="_ftnref42" title>[42]</a></p><p>This may have been a golden age for the Cayman Islands legal bar, which gladly incorporated hundreds of offshore foundation companies for crypto projects, but it was the dark ages for the United States. After the onslaught, few crypto firms remained in the country, each clinging to every word of Commissioner Hester Peirce’s dissenting statements to keep the faith.<a href="#_ftn43" name="_ftnref43" title>[43]</a></p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Hard Fork</strong></p><p>After President Trump took office last year, the President’s Working Group on Digital Asset Markets quickly instituted a hard fork from these Biden era policies.</p><p>SEC Chairman Atkins and I partnered together on Project Crypto to modernize our agencies’ rules and regulations to allow our markets to move onchain. As part of this initiative, the CFTC and SEC codified a joint interpretation to put Gary Gensler’s “embodiment theory” of security status to bed once and for all.<a href="#_ftn44" name="_ftnref44" title>[44]</a> Our joint interpretation classified crypto assets into five general categories: digital commodities,<a href="#_ftn45" name="_ftnref45" title>[45]</a> digital collectibles,<a href="#_ftn46" name="_ftnref46" title>[46]</a> digital tools,<a href="#_ftn47" name="_ftnref47" title>[47]</a> stablecoins,<a href="#_ftn48" name="_ftnref48" title>[48]</a> and digital securities.<a href="#_ftn49" name="_ftnref49" title>[49]</a> The interpretation clarified that the first three categories are generally not securities, stablecoins may in some cases be structured as securities, and digital securities are, of course, securities. The interpretation also explains how a non-security crypto asset offered or sold as part of an investment contract security may separate from the investment contract and no longer be subject to the federal securities laws.<a href="#_ftn50" name="_ftnref50" title>[50]</a></p><p>The SEC subsequently proposed Regulation Crypto Assets to establish a purpose-fit regulatory framework for offerings of investment contracts involving crypto assets and a security status “safe harbor” for crypto assets sold in these offerings.<a href="#_ftn51" name="_ftnref51" title>[51]</a> The administration delivered the clarity, certainty, and investor protections that crypto projects and participants demanded for American crypto asset distributions.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>A New Path Forward: Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM</strong></p><p>Now, I’m disappointed that Congress failed to deliver the Clarity Act to the President’s desk. This legislation would have codified in statute the line that Chairman Atkins and I have drawn between securities and non-securities, mandated that centralized crypto asset exchanges and brokerages register with the CFTC, and instituted purpose-fit core principles for these new CFTC registrants. But President Trump promised to deliver a crypto asset regulatory market structure with or without legislation, and we will help him deliver it using our existing statutory authorities.</p><p>Today, the CFTC is doing its part to deliver clear rules of the road for crypto asset markets with its advanced notice of proposed rulemaking on Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (Regulation CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (Regulation CAM), which is now live on the CFTC’s website. These rules would codify a pathway for crypto asset exchanges to operate under uniform national oversight by the CFTC pursuant to the same statutory authorities that the prior administration instead utilized to regulate by enforcement.</p><p>I want to underscore that this is a federal <em>option </em>for crypto asset exchanges. Just like the banking regulatory system, where firms may choose to pursue either a federal or state charter, with each type of charter authorizing the firm to engage in differing types of permissible activities, crypto firms should be free to pursue state licenses or federal registrations based upon the products and services the firm intends to offer. Only Congress has the authority to mandate that all crypto asset exchanges register with the Commission. However, Congress has mandated that exchanges that wish to offer retail customers the ability to trade crypto assets on a margined, leveraged, or financed basis register with the agency. But the agency never used this authority to issue purpose-fit rules for these transactions or platforms, only to enforce.</p><p>You might envision a ladder. On the first rung of the ladder are ordinary spot crypto exchanges (Rung 1 Exchanges), which are subject to the CFTC’s anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority but are otherwise generally regulated under state money transmission laws. On the second rung are exchanges that also offer retail customers the ability to trade crypto assets on a margined, leveraged, or financed basis (Rung 2 Exchanges), which are required to register with the CFTC and subject to its exclusive regulation. On the third rung are exchanges that also allow customers to trade perps and all other types of derivatives (Rung 3 Exchanges), which are also required to register with the CFTC and subject to its exclusive jurisdiction.</p><p>Today’s initial proposals would establish a regulatory framework for Rung 2 Exchanges—or firms offering retail customers the ability to trade crypto assets on a margined, leveraged, or financed basis. We refer to such a transaction as a CTX. Rung 3 Exchanges that are already registered with the CFTC as a DCM could begin offering trading in CTXs on their platforms under tailored rules. Non-registrants that wish to only offer CTXs could choose to either register as an ordinary DCM or pursue registration as a new sub-category of DCM called a “crypto asset market” (or CAM).</p><p>This provides firms with a clearer framework for evaluating how to best serve their customers in the United States and helps customers understand what protections apply to the platform they choose.</p><p>The CAM regime is designed for exchanges that only offer CTXs. To obtain designation as a CAM, an exchange would be required to adhere to the statutory DCM core principles, but with the benefit of a tailored set of regulations that are purpose-built and designed for CTXs. An exchange offering futures, options, or swaps would remain subject to the current DCM framework.</p><p>The statutory DCM core principles give us a sound starting point for the effective regulation of CAMs engaged in creating and administering national markets in CTXs. Principles 3 and 4 address contract listings and market surveillance.<a href="#_ftn52" name="_ftnref52" title>[52]</a> Principles 11 and 12 address financial integrity, customer funds, and abusive practices.<a href="#_ftn53" name="_ftnref53" title>[53]</a> Principles 16 and 20 address conflicts and system safeguards.<a href="#_ftn54" name="_ftnref54" title>[54]</a> For CAMs, the rules promulgated under these statutory obligations would address the specific risks posed by, and commercial realities of, CTXs.</p><p>For example, the statutory requirements of DCM Core Principle 3 require a CAM to show that a CTX is not readily susceptible to manipulation.<a href="#_ftn55" name="_ftnref55" title>[55]</a> However, the considerations in ensuring compliance with that statutory obligation with respect to CTXs differ from the considerations that are relevant to more traditional CFTC-regulated products. When listing CTXs, DCMs and CAMs may have to consider the distribution method and concentration of crypto assets, lock-ups periods and vesting schedules, whether there are programmatic issuances or buybacks, and a flurry of other crypto asset-specific considerations related to manipulation risks. Many crypto asset exchanges already voluntarily employ purpose-fit procedures to prevent the listing of crypto assets that are readily susceptible to manipulation. The proposed Regulation CAM regime would codify best practices into regulatory obligations that will serve the interests of American markets and their retail participants. Similarly, the Regulation CAM proposal also contemplates a “proof-of-reserves” obligation for exchanges that maintain customer property in omnibus accounts held for their customers’ benefit – a safeguard that I am sure would have benefitted FTX’s retail customers.&nbsp;</p><p>The proposed rules further contemplate the required intermediation of CTXs by a futures commission merchant (or FCM). Those FCMs would manage customer accounts and funds, subject to the CEA’s customer protection requirements, including disclosures,<a href="#_ftn56" name="_ftnref56" title>[56]</a><sup> </sup>capital requirements,<a href="#_ftn57" name="_ftnref57" title>[57]</a> and customer property segregation,<a href="#_ftn58" name="_ftnref58" title>[58]</a> among other areas. We are also examining and would welcome views on how FCM requirements should fit crypto asset activity while preserving clear responsibility for customer property, records, segregation, risk controls, and supervision. Requiring FCM intermediation of CTXs also ensures that customer-facing activity on a CAM would be subject to the Bank Secrecy Act’s (BSA) applicable anti-money laundering, customer identification, and suspicious activity reporting requirements, along with the various other related legal and regulatory obligations that the BSA and Commission regulations impose on FCMs.<a href="#_ftn59" name="_ftnref59" title>[59]</a></p><p>For those who prefer to do things the way the cypherpunks originally envisioned, we aim to provide the clarity needed for onchain finance to flourish. Our statute provides an exception to the on-exchange trading requirement for CTXs that involve “actual delivery” of the commodity within 28 days. We propose to codify an interpretation of “actual delivery” to clarify that delivery of a crypto asset to a user’s external, non-custodial digital wallet within 28 days generally satisfies this exception.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Onchain Finance</strong></p><p>And, another aside on onchain finance. Although outside the scope of today’s proposals, we are also exploring a durable policy for developers who publish software but do not solicit or take orders, control execution, or hold customer assets. A person should not have to register as an introducing broker simply because that person shipped code.</p><p>We are also working directly with builders to develop lawful pathways for onchain products in the United States. I’ve directed CFTC staff to engage with developers and founders to understand how onchain venues function, where control resides, how their activities compare to those performed by traditional market intermediaries, and how the CEA and our regulations apply to these new models.</p><p>American builders should have a clear path to bring new products to market here, under rules that protect customers and preserve market integrity, without sacrificing the features that make these technologies innovative in the first place.</p><p>And that brings me back to the broader purpose of the proposed framework I have outlined today.</p><p class="text-align-center"><strong>Golden Age</strong></p><p>As Professor Perez observed, technological revolutions have occurred and followed a similar course throughout human history. From the joint stock company to the railroad to the internet, new technologies are invariably dismissed, then abused by bad actors; there is a frenzy, a bubble, and an inevitable bust; at which point the technology has become common sense and regulators must craft rules for the new frontier. If the regulators get the rules right, they can usher in a golden age.</p><p>The framework I have outlined is an important step towards bringing crypto asset markets within the protections of the CEA. It will establish clear rules of the road for firms that want to serve American customers, strengthen the integrity of these markets, and provide a path for responsible innovation to take place here in America.</p><p>For years, entrepreneurs building on the new frontier of finance faced uncertainty about whether there was a place for them in our markets. We are giving them an answer.</p><p>Build here. Build markets that are open, competitive, and worthy of the public’s trust. Build under American rules and American standards. And build knowing that responsible innovation has a place in the United States.</p><p>Satoshi’s technological revolution has transformed global financial markets. If America can embrace this paradigm shift and get the right regulations in place, we can usher in a golden age like those that followed the transformative technologies of the past.<a href="#_ftn60" name="_ftnref60" title>[60]</a></p><p>Thank you, and I look forward to the fireside chat to follow.&nbsp;</p><hr align="left" size="1" width="33%"><div id="ftn1"><p><a href="#_ftnref1" name="_ftn1" title>[1]</a> <em>Virtual Currencies: The Oversight Role of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission</em>: <em>Hearing Before the S. <span>WSJ Op-Ed | CFTC’s New Rules for Crypto</span>

            <div class="field field--name-body field--type-text-with-summary field--label-hidden field--item"><p>Washington long debated whether crypto was the future of finance or merely a fad. Meanwhile, American entrepreneurs built, investors put their capital to work and markets evolved faster than the rules governing them. Congress considered legislation to clarify the treatment of crypto assets under federal law and regulate firms in these markets, but failed to send a bill to the president’s desk. Fortunately, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) have the statutory authority to issue rules and regulations establishing a federal crypto regulatory market structure. Today, the CFTC is proposing its first round of regulations for crypto markets.</p><p>Under the prior administration, the CFTC and SEC targeted crypto exchanges, custodians and software developers for alleged failures to comply with laws and regulations. Rather than use their authority to issue new rules to account for the innovation occurring in our markets, the two agencies chose to regulate through enforcement. In response, many crypto asset firms fled the U.S. for foreign shores.</p><p>One was Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX, the now-defunct Bahamas-based crypto asset exchange infamous for its meteoric rise and tumultuous downfall. FTX imploded after its founders fraudulently misappropriated approximately $8 billion in customer funds to finance their own proprietary investments. Only after the firm failed did the CFTC and SEC charge FTX and its founders for wrongdoing.</p><p>FTX and many other failed crypto platforms, like BlockFi and Voyager Digital, operated in the U.S. via subsidiaries with state money-transmitter licenses. Unlike federal agencies, state agencies have accommodated crypto intermediaries within their statutory frameworks for more than a decade. However, state money-transmitter laws aren’t uniform and are intended for payment-services providers rather than financial markets, which have historically been regulated by the CFTC and SEC. Federal regulations require trading venues to meet stringent standards to deter manipulation and abusive trading practices, ensure orderly and transparent trading, prevent conflicts of interest and safeguard customer funds.</p><p>Most of the offshore and state-regulated FTX corporate entities went bankrupt, but the customer property held by its CFTC-registered subsidiary remained segregated and secure.</p><p>The lesson should have been obvious. America doesn’t need to choose between responsible innovation and the protection all market participants need from fraudulent and abusive practices. It needs prophylactic rules that reasonably ensure both.</p><p>Instead, during the Biden administration, regulatory uncertainty became a defining feature of crypto-asset markets. Rather than establishing clear rules, the CFTC and SEC pursued a post-hoc regulation-by-enforcement approach that was overwhelmed by trillions of dollars in transaction volume. The result was uncertainty for legitimate businesses and, more important, an environment that would encourage the development of more FTXs.</p><p>Following the Senate’s failure to advance the Clarity Act this month, the CFTC is proposing rule-making concerning Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (Regulation CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (Regulation CAM). This follows a joint interpretation by the CFTC and SEC earlier this year, which clarified that a swath of crypto assets, including bitcoin and ether, are non-securities within the CFTC’s regulatory authority.</p><p>Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM would establish requirements for CFTC-registered exchanges that offer these crypto assets for trading. Unlike the Clarity Act, these regulations wouldn’t require crypto assets to trade on CFTC-registered platforms. We don’t have the authority to impose such a requirement without congressional action. However, the rules would establish a purpose-fit option for crypto-asset exchanges that wish to operate under a single federal market-regulatory scheme. Unlike state-licensed exchanges, these exchanges would be permitted to allow retail customers to trade on a margined, leveraged or financed basis. Such platforms are distinct from ordinary spot-trading venues and are squarely within the CFTC’s regulatory jurisdiction.</p><p>Former SEC Chairman Gary Gensler glibly told crypto exchanges to “come in and register.” The exchanges would have had to concede that the crypto assets on their platforms were securities and operate under legacy rules and regulations designed for vastly different infrastructure. Those days are over. The CFTC is moving quickly to institute rules and regulations that account for the distinctions between crypto assets and other types of commodities.</p><p>Today’s action is just the beginning. The CFTC is starting the process of addressing gaps in crypto-asset market structure and creating clear rules of the road for innovators and market participants. We haven’t solved every problem, nor can agency action substitute indefinitely for a statutory framework passed by Congress, but we must do what we can.</p><p>America can lead the next generation of financial technology without repeating the mistakes of the last one: President Trump has made that clear.</p><p>The last chapter of crypto regulation was written by crisis. The new frontier of finance will be written by opportunity, innovation and clear rules.</p></div>
